extracted.intended_audience: school administrators, Title IX coordinators, legal counsel, and policy stakeholders involved in implementing or enforcing Title IX in K-12 and higher education
extracted.subtask_description: Federal Department of Education preamble explaining the final regulatory definition of 'sexual harassment' under §106.30, including its three prongs (quid pro quo; Davis standard; Clery Act/VAWA offenses), interpretive guidance, scope limitations, and implementation implications for recipients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct 'on the basis of sex' (introductory element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether conduct is 'on the basis of sex' does not require probing the subjective motive of the respondent; where conduct is sexual in nature, or where conduct references one sex or another, that suffices to constitute conduct 'on the basis of sex.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department follows the Supreme Court's approach (Gebser, Davis) interpreting conduct 'on the basis of sex' to include conduct of a sexual nature or conduct referencing/aimed at a particular sex. The final §106.30 moves the phrase 'on the basis of sex' to the introductory sentence applying to all three prongs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prong 1 — Quid pro quo harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Quid pro quo harassment: making educational benefits or opportunities contingent on a person's participation in unwelcome conduct on the basis of sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies whether the 'bargain' is communicated expressly or impliedly; does not require subjective intent by the employee to deny aid or benefit; a complainant's acquiescence to avoid negative consequences does not mean prohibited quid pro quo did not occur. The Department declines to require quid pro quo to be severe or pervasive because a single instance of abuse of authority can jeopardize equal educational access. The quid pro quo prong applies to the recipient's employees (the Department declined to expand it to non-employee students, volunteers, vendors, etc.), though unwelcome conduct by non-employees may fall under other prongs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unwelcome element is subjective
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'unwelcome' as used in the first and second prongs of §106.30 is a subjective element; a complainant's subjective statement that the conduct was unwelcome suffices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a complainant pretended to welcome conduct (e.g., out of fear of negative consequences), the complainant's later subjective statement that the conduct was unwelcome meets the element. This subjective standard applies to both quid pro quo and hostile-environment analyses under §106.30.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prong 2 — Davis standard (severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive; denial of equal access)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actionable hostile-environment sexual harassment is conduct that is severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive such that it effectively denies a person equal access to the recipient's education program or activity (the Davis formulation adopted as the second prong).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department adopts Davis for administrative enforcement to provide consistency with private litigation while avoiding chilling protected speech. The elements are determined under a reasonable person standard. The Department rejects the view that the Davis standard precludes totality-of-the-circumstances analysis and expects recipients to consider relevant factors (e.g., ages, number of parties, positions of authority, disability status). The second prong addresses non-quid pro quo, non-Clery/VAWA offenses and is intended to focus on conduct that meaningfully deprives equal educational access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable person standard for Davis elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The elements in the Davis standard (severe, pervasive, objectively offensive, and denial of equal access) are determined under a reasonable person standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarification was added to §106.30 so that recipients evaluate Davis elements from the perspective of a reasonable person considering the totality of circumstances rather than a purely subjective-only or erratic standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prong 3 — Clery Act/VAWA offenses (sexual assault, dating violence, domestic violence, stalking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual assault and other sex-based violence offenses (as described in the Clery Act and VAWA) constitute sexual harassment under §106.30 and are treated as conduct that is assumed to deny equal access to education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such offenses do not have to be evaluated for severity, pervasiveness, or offensiveness; they are by definition serious and actionable. For students who are underage, statutory rape or other Clery-defined sex offenses count as sexual harassment even if the victim nominally consented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of actors for quid pro quo vs other prongs
rubrics_metrics.description: The quid pro quo prong reasonably holds recipients responsible for conduct of the recipient's employees and does not expand liability to all agents of a recipient (e.g., non-employee students, volunteers, vendors), though unwelcome conduct by non-employees may be addressed under the second or third prongs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department relies on Gebser's statutory/agency reasoning to limit quid pro quo employer-like liability to employees; commenters' requests to expand to non-employees were declined, but recipients still may be responsible under other prongs for non-employee conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual knowledge and deliberate indifference (recipient responsibilities)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department's framework defines actual knowledge broadly (including notice to any Title IX Coordinator and any elementary or secondary school employee) and applies a deliberate indifference standard that requires recipients to respond appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final regulations require that a recipient offer supportive measures to a complainant, for the Title IX Coordinator to discuss supportive measures with a complainant (with or without a formal complaint), and to explain the process for filing a formal complaint. These adaptations broaden recipients' obligations compared with some judicial applications of Gebser/Davis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dismissal under Title IX does not preclude other code-of-conduct responses
rubrics_metrics.description: If a formal complaint is dismissed because the alleged conduct does not meet the §106.30 definition of sexual harassment, that dismissal is for purposes of Title IX only and does not preclude the recipient from responding to the allegations under the recipient's own code of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.45(b)(3)(i) was revised to clarify this point so recipients may still address misconduct through non-Title IX disciplinary or conduct processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid chilling protected speech; balance First Amendment concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition and standards should avoid chilling protected speech and academic freedom; the Davis standard helps ensure that speech and expressive conduct are not peremptorily chilled while permitting punishment when speech becomes serious enough to lose First Amendment protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department intentionally rooted the definition in Supreme Court framework to provide precise standards that limit over-broad regulation of speech in higher education settings and avoid prior restraints; this is a rationale for preferring Davis over looser guidance definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use totality-of-the-circumstances and contextual factors in evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluations of whether conduct rises to actionable sexual harassment under the Davis standard depend on a constellation of factors and the totality of circumstances (including ages, number of parties, disability status, positions of authority, and other factors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department expressly allows and expects recipients to apply common-sense, holistic analyses; nothing in the final regulations disallows the usual balancing of relevant factors used by courts and guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department preference for precise definition over looser earlier guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department prefers the Davis-based definition (unwelcome conduct on the basis of sex that is severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive and effectively denies equal access) as it provides more precise standards than the looser 'unwelcome conduct of a sexual nature'/'sufficiently serious' language used in prior departmental guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department believes the precision reduces chilling of speech and unnecessary intervention, while providing clarity for recipients — though recipients retain flexibility to address misconduct outside Title IX through other codes. The Department declined to re-list the 2001 Guidance 'Factors Used to Evaluate Hostile Environment' because §106.30's elements and reasonable person standard are intended to guide application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concerns raised by commenters for broader, victim-protective standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Many commenters urged adoption of broader definitions (e.g., the 2001 Guidance or 'unwelcome conduct of a sexual nature' that is 'sufficiently serious that it interferes with or limits a student's ability to participate in or benefit from the school's programs') and argued the Davis 'and' requirement (severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive) would deter reporting and exclude many harmful incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects stakeholder evaluative criteria: prioritize low reporting barriers, avoid raising thresholds that force survivors to 'quantify' suffering, consider cultural/pervasive harms that may be comprised of numerous individually minor incidents, and err on the side of a zero-tolerance approach. The Department considered these comments but adopted the Davis-based approach with specified adaptations.
